source.title: Strategic Attentive Writer for Learning Macro-Actions
source.authors: Alexander; Vezhnevets; Volodymyr Mnih; J. Agapiou; Simon Osindero; Alex Graves; O. Vinyals; K. Kavukcuoglu

page_placements.theme: Explicit planning modules or planning tokens in RL and sequence agents

record.tranche_reason: Tests learned multi-step plans in a next-character task and in navigation/game environments, using STRAW's explicit action-plan and commitment mechanism rather than the claim's hidden-state probing or rhyme intervention.
record.gate_note: The text reports frequent four-character macro-actions and qualitative navigation/game replanning. Atari score comparisons and maze transfer rewards are not rows because those metrics do not themselves measure the future-token or look-ahead behaviour.
record.test_reason: STRAW builds a multi-step action plan into the architecture: an explicit plan matrix plus a commitment mechanism. Its macro-actions are therefore produced by design. The study does not measure look-ahead arising in ordinary next-token models, hidden-state decodability, pre-caching, or emergent look-ahead. This is the 'induces the behaviour on purpose' case, so it does not test any version. Its findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim STRAW advances state-of-the-art scores on several Atari games that need extended planning and exploration, and that learned commitment beats replanning every step or at random intervals.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a purpose-built recurrent architecture with an explicit action-plan matrix and commitment-plan, trained to learn macro-actions. It does not probe or intervene on a conventional language model's hidden-state representation.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and environment affect the learned plans: the paper describes shorter macro-actions near danger in Amidar and frequent replanning in Breakout, where precise control is useful.

fits_no_version.finding: An RL and sequence architecture with an explicit, attentively written action-plan matrix and a learned commitment schedule learns macro-actions. In text these resemble frequent 4-grams; in mazes the agent replans at corners and junctions; in Atari it shows high-level action chunks and shorter commitment near enemies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectures with an explicit multi-step plan state learn useful temporally extended macro-actions and adaptive replanning points from data.

record.problems: The next-character result is qualitative and reports no numerical rank values or uncertainty. STRAW is specifically designed to maintain and commit to plans, so this does not establish that ordinary language models spontaneously use such plans. The navigation and Atari examples are qualitative and do not test token-level language behaviour.
record.rows_left_out: Atari scores in Table 1 and maze transfer rewards in Figure 3.b are performance measures, not direct measures of look-ahead or pre-cached token representations.

untested.parts: All: no verse, rhyme words or frontier LLM.
All: no decoding of future tokens from a single hidden state of a standard model.
All: no test of whether standard models compute features for later positions. STRAW's plan is imposed by the architecture.
All: no open-weight language model or attribution and probing tools.
All: no measurement of internal look-ahead emerging in reasoning, chess or Sokoban models. Maze and Atari plans are architectural.
All: no test of plan depth or of whether plans are incidental local features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2 'tests' assignment and its supports labels for V3 and V5 are removed. Plans that exist because the architecture builds them in cannot show that models plan ahead internally. This is a 2016 pre-transformer architecture paper; it is relevant background only.

versions.untested_parts: No rhyming verse, candidate rhyme words, or intervention changing an intended rhyme.
No test of whether a single hidden state can decode tokens several positions ahead.

The study tests an explicitly designed STRAW plan in next-character prediction, not whether ordinary models compute such features as a side effect of next-token training. It does not intervene on a cached feature to measure its effect on intervening characters.
No open-weight model or open attribution-graph or probing tool is tested.
The study examines maze navigation and Atari games, not multi-step reasoning, chess, or Sokoban; it does not test language-model look-ahead in those tasks.
The study does not test whether apparent plans are incidental local features or whether they causally steer generation as opposed to serving as explicit plans.

rows.subject: STRAW
rows.operation_detail: Recorded character sequences emitted while STRAW was committed to its action-plan; compared frequent length-4 macro-actions with Penn Treebank 4-gram frequency ranks.
rows.measure: Correspondence between macro-action frequency rank and actual 4-gram frequency rank
rows.value: Authors describe the macro-actions as corresponding to common n-grams; examples include 'the', 'ing' and 'and'. Figure 3.c plots the ranks for the 20 most frequent length-4 macro-actions.
rows.note: The model is an LSTM with a STRAW module on top. The plan is explicitly maintained during commitment; this is not a test of an ordinary language model's hidden state.
rows.check: The plan is an architectural action-plan matrix, not a feature computed incidentally in a standard model's hidden state. It cannot bear on V3's 'computed because it helps later positions' versus side-effect question. Subject is an LSTM with a STRAW module on top. The listed macro-actions are 4-character strings that include spaces (e.g. '_the', 'ing_'). The figure gives no numeric rank values.

rows.subject: STRAWe
rows.operation_detail: Visualized where the agent terminated macro-actions and replanned.

conditions.value: 11 x 11 random maze; evaluation on a fixed-geometry maze with varying start and goal locations

rows.measure: Replanning events by maze cell, normalized by total visits to the cell
rows.value: Figure only; the text says corners and areas close to junctions are highlighted.
rows.note: This is qualitative evidence of temporally extended action plans in navigation, not a language-model result.
rows.check: This is replanning in an RL agent built with an explicit plan module, not internal look-ahead emerging in a network. Figure only, no numbers.

rows.subject: STRAW
rows.operation_detail: Visualized the agent's replanning and changes to its action-plan as an enemy approached and blocked its path.
rows.measure: Qualitative replanning behaviour and macro-action duration
rows.value: The text describes the agent retreating when blocked, resuming its earlier plan when the path clears, and planning shorter macro-actions while the enemy is near.
rows.note: The paper describes the example qualitatively; no numerical effect is reported.
rows.check: A single qualitative Amidar example of replanning in an explicit-plan architecture. It is not a measure of emergent look-ahead.

relation.reason: The study addresses related temporal planning concepts through its own explicit-plan architecture; it neither tests nor uses the catalog's claimed internal look-ahead finding.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates a purpose-built action-plan and commitment architecture, with a loss encouraging commitment. It does not test planning arising otherwise, future-token decoding from ordinary hidden states, or pre-caching as distinguished from next-token side effects.

source_check.notes: The qualitative findings and authors' conclusion are supported. Frostbite attribution differs between the Figure 4 caption, which says STRAW, and the accompanying text, which specifies STRAWe.
